comments.name: John S
comments.body: One problem is that validating late ballots depends on the postmark date. But the Postal Service has adopted a final rule (FR Doc. 2025-20740) adding section 608.11 to the Domestic Mail Manual. The new section states, “…the postmark date does not necessarily indicate the first day that the Postal Service had possession of the mailpiece. Moreover, … the Postal Service does not postmark all mail in the ordinary course of operations.” “Because most postmarks are applied at processing facilities, they do not necessarily represent either the place at which, or the date on which, the Postal Service first accepted possession of the mailpiece. The date inscribed by a postmark applied at a processing facility may be later than the date that the mailpiece was first accepted by the Postal Service.” Since the USPS is under the control of Trump, I will not be surprised if boxes of late ballots are put on the shelf in certain post offices and then (oops) postmarked after Election Day.

I have ADHD (diagnosed from neuropsychological testing done as a child and retesting as an adult, each lasting for ~8 hours and done by neuropsychologists). I see this same phenomenon online when it comes to ADHD.

It’s beyond infuriating how often people on social media talk about their “ADHD” symptoms like forgetting where they put their keys, their preferences for being on their phone instead of doing a task they’re dreading, getting energized when they’re excited, or restless in lengthy and boring meetings. These are all normal human experiences. EVERYONE does this.

But there is all this narrative about “adult onset ADHD” (which isn’t a thing) and how every person who is otherwise very successful but occasionally forgets they had an appointment or an item off their shopping list must be “masking”.

And then of course others read this and think, “hey I do this” and think they have ADHD. It does not help that so many family doctors hand out prescriptions based on them answering a few questions where the answer is obvious. There’s even online businesses that will diagnose someone and send them meds in an ongoing subscription model. Others don’t even bother with this low bar and claim to be self-diagnosed.

They treat ADHD as a quirky trait, when in reality living with the disorder is hell. I hate having ADHD so much, and I cannot stand when people trivialize it. The online ADHD discourse is doing so much damage to a disorder that’s already hugely misunderstood.

By their standard, deals of deli type specialities suggest more of a sybaritic lifestyle, to which they are not accustomed. Some years ago, I went in to a Costco store, having just finished work on a grubby project, not having time to dress more in the convention I described. AI is simply following the General Purpose Technology Productivity, "J curve" and with this story, I think we've just hit the, "Trough" and are commencing the, "Upswing" which is wonderful news.

I work in tech/software which has been massively disrupted (as you would expect) by AI over the pat 3 years with significant layoffs, but to me this looks like we're finally seeing the, "Upward trajectory" of additional economic productivity because of AI.

What is a General Purpose Technology (GPT)? A GPT is a technology that:

Is widely applicable across industries.Improves over time.Enables complementary innovations and new business processes, often times a major, "Once in a generation" new technology.

Historical examples include:Steam enginesElectrificationComputingThe Internet(And now) Artificial Intelligence

Historical examples:

ElectricityFactories initially saw little improvement when they simply replaced steam engines with electric motors.Productivity surged only after factories were redesigned around electric power.

Computers and the InternetMassive IT spending in the 1980s and early 1990s produced limited measured gains.Significant productivity growth appeared in the late 1990s after firms reorganized work around digital technologies.

Bottom line (in my judgement) we're, "Turning the corner" and I predict significant productivity (and hiring) gains over the next 12-24 months. (And beyond of course.)

comments.name: James Thorleifson
comments.body:
Boy howdy, I am sick to death of our government minders minding my own business. I live on a Copano Bay on the Texas Coastal Bend. I have a 250 foot long pier. I spend quite a bit a bit of time out there on the deck at the end of the pier, and my WiFi doesn’t reach that far. So I’m looking into installing a directional wireless access point, so I can enjoy the WSJ whilst sipping coffee out at the end of my pier. Only to discover, in the course of my product research, that foreign providers of routers and whatnot are now effectively banned from the U.S. market due to fears of Chinese spying.

Now, wireless access points aren’t subject to the ban, since they operate behind whatever router you might have. But if foreign companies are banned from supplying networking mainstays like routers, it’s entirely likely they may exit the U.S. market entirely. Potentially leaving me with an artificially obsolescent and unsupported piece of equipment. So, now I’ve got to take that possibility into account in my product selection. Gee, thanks for nuthin’ Uncle Sam. 😑

Here’s a crazy idea. How about our government treats us like functioning adults, and lets us make our own choices about the products we use. Believe it or not, I, and just about every other responsible adult in this country, is perfectly capable of assessing the level of risk I am willing to tolerate in any product.

I don't think China likes using bullets and bombs but they do like control. The sleeping dragon is now awake and much depends on its next moves. The loss of oil is no small pain point. China is still heavily dependent on oil and remains the top global crude oil importer, the disruption of supplies from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Iran and Venezuela is not making the dragon happy. China has actively accelerated its purchases of Russian crude and is drawing down its massive strategic petroleum reserves (estimated at 1.3 to 1.5 billion barrels). This self-sufficiency has effectively kept global oil prices from spiraling completely out of control. If that supply runs too low I would suspect a global recession at a minimum. 

This is a very precarious scenario. The U.S. would be wise to cut its losses and complexly withdraw military forces from the mideast. This ignores the fact that fluid and water balance is a problem that has been present for hundreds of millions of years, more critical even since coming out onto land, and that the kidney and brainstem have been working on it under penalty of death (or non-reproduction). 

This is a bit like reading a article about how to "breathe right" while ignoring the fact that you have a brainstem that is managing this all the time. 

Fortunately, it is not up to your cerebral cortex to have to mange this, for 95% of people.  If you drink a reasonable amount of fluids, your kidney and ancient brain will figure it out.    I doubt that any other animal on the planet is spending even a moment figuring out how much to drink and whether their diet is "hydrating" enough, yet somehow they seem OK. The same happens with thirst.  When your body needs hydration, hydration will be the ONLY thing your body thinks about after breathing.  Every moment you spend will be to find water.

In general, it would boil down to two separate issues:

A. The AI vehicle made a mistake.

B. The AI was specifically programmed to overlook traffic rules in some instances. 

For cases of A, that is understandable. This is nascent tech and the builders will, hopefully, take the data and refine the algorithms.

For cases of B, this is where society needs to keep a close eye on the tech. There are clear cases where the car needs to make decisions that would violate traffic rules (it is okay to go over the double yellow line if the car has to swerve to miss something in the road, for example),  but these cars should be programmed to generally be "perfect" when things are not an emergent situation.

There is (currently) no public recourse in finding out why these cars did what they did. If it were a human, you could ask them "why did you park like that?" . But there is no way for anyone right now to ask Waymo "why did your car do that?" and get a real answer. As the world shifts toward these autonomous cars, I don't care about the fine for each of these violations, what would be more effective is if the company was required (for every violation) to submit a report detailing why the car did what it did and what  the company is doing to correct the error.

The devastating heatwaves currently fracturing Europe are a grim demonstration of climate change as a systems-level crisis where history, infrastructure, and human biology collide. There is a profound, tragic irony unfolding here: while the Global South is often forced into a carbon-heavy trap by an immediate infrastructural necessity to use cheap fossil fuels, Europe is now reaping the atmospheric whirlwind of the West’s historical emission legacy.
The current crisis proves that no amount of wealth creates a shield against a warped planet. Through El Niño teleconnections, a thermal anomaly thousands of miles away in the Pacific has distorted the jet stream, pinning a lethal, compressed heat dome directly over European cities.
This is where the historical infrastructure trap springs shut on Europe itself. For centuries, European buildings were engineered exclusively to retain heat, not repel it. When temperatures breach 37°C, these insulated structures become urban ovens. Stripped of the melanin shield that their ancestors evolutionary shed to survive in a low-sunlight environment, these unacclimatized populations face rapid, systemic physiological failure. The thousands of excess deaths recorded this summer are the direct result of an evolutionary and structural paradigm failing in real time. The infrastructure divide hasn't just left the developing world vulnerable; it has rendered the developed world an architectural trap.

comments.name: Kelly Grace Smith
comments.body:
20 years ago Stanford and places in Japan had technology addiction programs; kept quiet here because there were billions to be made.

As a communications professional and leadership/personal development coach, I began writing about the impact of technology 18 years ago...people thought I was crazy.

You did not need to be an "expert" or a scientist to see the addictive nature of technology and with it, social media. You just needed your common sense.

(And you needed to be willing to spend significant periods of time each day...separated from technology.)

Therein lies the problem; too much time spent on technology begins to limit our awarenesses, our common sense, oour critical thinking, our creativity and productivity.

The energy buzz you get from technology - your emotional and mental functions resonating with the speed of the internet - makes you "feel" like you are productive, but in fact, how could your real life productivity be better...when you are spending more and more time on technology?

The bottom line is this...

Life is about experience, real life experiences...within ourselves as a result of our contact and connection with others and with the world around us.

Time spent on technology takes time away from...real life experience.

Experience is the seed bed that cultivates wisdom, connection, creativity, empathy...and healthy relationships.

The "tool" of technology has become our master. Now, we must learn to use it in moderation and get back to real life.

I guess its actual value might be in things like pharmacological or astronomical research and data analysis, or in controlling traffic lights in the most efficient manner, but as far as I know, there haven't been any triumphs of this nature reported.

Meanwhile, there has been a vast pollution of our communication networks with low-value AI-created junk, and it will only get worse. There are countless instances of academic and professional fraud. Lawyers are getting disbarred. Copyright is being violated on a grand scale. People are losing their grip on reality.

In this context, why do all these opinion pieces as though this technology has justified its reason to exist at all?

comments.name: Wondering
comments.body:
I'm a professor who studies and uses AI. I've spent several years observing students increasingly fall into two polarized groups (I'll exclude intentional cheaters here):  Those who unintentionally overuse AI because they don't understand where the authorship line is.  And those who reject AI completely, dogmatically assuming that any use of AI automatically obliterates all authorship.   

Both groups need to learn a more nuanced, mature understanding.  My approach would be to start teaching it at a younger age from a media literacy approach: i.e., how do we understand authorship.  How do LLMs work?  Where is the data sourced from? Let's do some exercises to see what biases / assumptions might lie in the dataset.   What is the impact of algorithms vs. the dataset?   How can we create our own AI tools so we can take some control/authorship over the AI systems we use?  etc.   I do this with my university students, but a lot of it can/should start at a younger age. Just as we (hopefully) start media literacy at a younger age, so students learn not to take all the media they consume at face value. 

These approaches would help not only the group that struggles to avoid overuse, but also the students who reject AI entirely and without nuance. I'm actually more concerned about this group, not because I think they "need to learn AI."  I'm concerned because it's important to learn how to critically evaluate nuanced, controversial topics — not stick one's fingers in one's ears.

AI cannot distinguish nuance (although, to be candid, all too many people can't either) which is so essential for understanding and solving the many challanges that face us. comments.body: Study of the Kaballah perhaps represents a journey rather than a destination, which is why it is a useful analogue. Because if AI simply deposits you at a destination, there is of course no journey, you will arrive as you left with no intervening process of discovery, and all your steps remain a black box of mystery and groundless uncertainty. You are left unable to retrace your path, understand your progress, correct any mis-direction. You are thereby consigned to faith rather than understanding. I think that is the lesson of Kaballah, because faith without understanding has led many astray and was I think the basis of concerns. It is as applicable in software programming as it is with language and idea generation. It concerns me that AI has now exceeded human understanding of its operations. And that's just first order, never mind AI programming AI, iteratively into oblivion.

comments.name: Jaganathan
comments.body:
The traditional restriction studying Kabbalah before 40 stems from a fear that its intense, non-dualistic abstractions would shatter an ungrounded mind. The theory was that one needed a lifetime of framework—a "vessel"—before handling this "light." But there is a glaring flaw here: waiting until the worldview is already fixed removes the power of wisdom to shape the mind’s fundamental architecture. True systemic wisdom belongs in the formative windows (ages 8–14) when ethics and causality are wired, not as an afterthought to a rigid intellect.This maps perfectly onto how we must approach AI through a graded introduction.Up to age 11, LLMs are a cognitive crutch. If machine generates the prose, a child misses the organic struggle of syntax and vocabulary retrieval, leaving a shallow internal processing engine. Once the mind transitions into advanced science, the constraint shifts from text generation to conceptual synthesis.
If a student is analyzing why light travels at a constant velocity, using AI to draft the essay doesn't bypass the work. The human mind must still possess the conceptual architecture to validate and comprehend the physics. Restricting AI at this stage starves the intellect of the scale needed for advanced thought. Kabbalah teaches that unconstrained light shatters a weak vessel. The solution isn't to withhold the light until the vessel is  brittle; it is to build a robust internal container early so it can direct infinite data without shattering.

I found this story misleading and disappointing. When many people hear “save the bees,” they assume that means helping honeybees. However, honeybees are managed agricultural animals and are not endangered in the U.S. Native bees are the ones facing serious decline; they are also essential to the ecosystems, pollinating plants far beyond agriculture.

Instead of quoting a facility manager’s well-intentioned but scientifically incomplete view, The Times could have quoted ecological experts to educate readers about how to truly help native bees instead: restoring habitat with native plants, and reducing pesticide spraying that harms the pollinators.

Two local resources for more information on the importance of native bees and the impact of European Honey bees would be the Riverside Park Conservancy, and NYC Pollinators (noting their Policy Statement about European Honey Bees). There has already been so much damage to the existing ecosystem. The NYT can do better.

comments.body: The bearding is not because there are so many bees but because it's so hot out. Just as New Yorkers would sit on the stoop (before air conditioning), bees move out of the hive when it's too hot inside. They're removing their own heat, making space for ventilation to cool the hive, and helping with ventilation by beating their wings and moving air into and out of the entrance. Workers actually carry water to the hive and then evaporate it by beating their wings. Honeybees invented evaporative cooling! After the hive cools down, they'll all move back inside.

"People who are not professional historians sometimes assume that historical research is a once-and-for-all process that will eventually produce a single, final version of what happened in the past. But revisiting and often revising earlier interpretations is actually at the very core of what historians do. And that’s because the present is continually changing." 
https://ncph.org/what-is-public-history/how-historians-work/the-changing-past/
[National Council on Public History]

History is chaotic and particularly for the span of our lifetimes.

We are too close to readily understand the events.   Where in a Nation one is may expose different local standards for textbooks or even different attitudes in differing communities within a State or a Canadian Province.   How Alberta sees the Canadian Dominion likely is quite different from that way Quebec sees matters.    I expect that events in Paris or in Arles or in Champagne see different takes within France.

History is a mish-mosh of holdings and the Black community has its various takes even amongst its generation.

comments.name: Kathryn Hurdman
comments.body: I often use old travel journals when I write about my travels, and I'm surprised at some of the things I've remembered incorrectly. It's fun to write from memory and then go back and see what actually happened! I wish I would have kept even more detailed journals and will use a lot of these ideas. I like the idea of adding color/visuals and also exploring a place by looking for flaws or fonts!

comments.name: Wayne
comments.body: My biggest advice as someone who has journaled for years is, unless you are well into the practice go with slimmer volumes. It will not feel as daunting to fill. They make multi year journals do not recommend these as inevitably  you are going to loose or spill something on a journal.better to loose a week's work than years.a lot of ppl start to journal but drop it quickly because they feel their entries are meh. Don't get bogged down in trying to make it read as if a novel, just jott impressions,  make it impressionistic

comments.name: Metaphor
comments.body: I am downsizing from a four-bedroom house to a two-bedroom condo. The amount of stuff that went either to recycling, the estate sale, or in the trash is astounding.  The last thing I need is more physical possessions. From now on, when I travel I think I will be content to re-visit my journeys by looking at my digital photos.

comments.name: Randy Stone
comments.body: My husband and I have over 30 travel journals compiled from all our trips. they include pictures, hiking maps, stories of the places we went and the people we met, restaurant slips and menus, Museum tickets. Total joy. We collect items in a plastic bag, only write a one pager for the day, and then when we are home, we look at our pictures we build the narrative and the stories.

comments.name: LL
comments.body: I now use Apple’s Day One app, which allows me to include photos and text. I photograph my art, adding that also. The published book is a beautiful keepsake. I create travel journals for specific trips and journals for daily life, each covering six months at a time. Using this app has been transformational.

comments.name: Neil
comments.body: I wouldn’t defend xenophobia of any kind, but you have to look at the history and context of South Africa. Yes, the economy and country is more developed than many in the continent, but there has been a significant failure in governments in enabling its citizens (particularly black South Africans) to share some of the fruits of that development. That was likely many had hoped for post-1994, but it hasn’t come to pass. As a result people have become frustrated and as in many countries across the world, resorted to scapegoating migrants. I’m not condoning or justifying the xenophobia, but the history can help why it’s a little different to the rest of the continent. It’s also somewhat suspect how the latest events seem so well coordinated and appear to be well funded, suggesting there might be some malign external influence.
